section_title: Why does heaven never stop worshiping God?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 7 The first living creature was like a lion, the second like a calf, the third had a face like a man, and the fourth was like an eagle in flight. 8 And each of the four living creatures had six wings and was covered with eyes all around and within. Day and night they never stop saying: “Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!”

9 And whenever the living creatures give glory, honor, and thanks to the One seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever, 10 the twenty-four elders fall down before the One seated on the throne, and they worship Him who lives forever and ever. They cast their crowns before the throne, saying: 11 “Worthy are You, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for You created all things; by Your will they exist and were created.”

context_lines: The description of the four living creatures continues from verse 6. John sees likenesses of a lion, a calf, a human face and a flying eagle. Each creature has six wings and is covered with eyes. These are images within a vision of God’s throne, with close connections to earlier Scripture.

[Ezekiel 1:5–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/ezekiel/1.htm) describes four living creatures with related faces, though their arrangement and wings differ. [Ezekiel 10:20–22](https://biblehub.com/bsb/ezekiel/10.htm) identifies those creatures as cherubim. The six wings and repeated declaration of God’s holiness also recall the seraphim in [Isaiah 6:1–3](https://biblehub.com/bsb/isaiah/6.htm). John’s scene brings these familiar images together.

The creatures continually praise God as holy, almighty and eternally living. The elders respond by falling before Him, worshiping and placing their crowns before His throne. Whatever honor they possess is offered back to the One they worship.

Their spoken reason is creation: all things owe their existence to God’s will. Before the vision moves into the opening of the seals, it fixes attention on the worthiness of the Creator. Heaven’s worship gives a perspective from which to hear the difficult scenes ahead.
common_interpretation_lines: Interpretations differ over what the creatures represent. The [USCCB notes](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/revelation/4) understand them as representing creation, with the lion, calf, human and eagle expressing its varied strengths. [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-revelation-of-jesus-christ/) connects them with heavenly powers and considers their representation of the Christian church. [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/revelation/4.htm) favors gospel ministers, applying their features to courage, patient service, understanding and readiness. These are different explanations of the imagery; the creatures’ worship of God is clear in all of them.

Wesley hears the repeated holiness as praise of the triune God: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Gill likewise applies the praise to all three. Both understand the elders’ action as humble acknowledgment that God deserves the honor He has given His people. The scene directs attention toward Him, even where readers differ about the identity of those around the throne.
god_plan_lines: [Psalm 148](https://biblehub.com/bsb/psalms/148.htm) calls the heavens, angels, earth, living creatures and peoples to praise the LORD because He created them. Revelation’s throne-room worship belongs to that larger movement: creation acknowledging the One to whom it owes its life.

The vision does not begin with earthly evil as the center of reality. It begins with the Creator’s throne and the worship He deserves. That prepares for the next chapter, where the song will also celebrate the Lamb’s work of redemption. Creation and redemption come together in the unfolding vision, giving reason for worship before the judgments begin.
